source_sentences.text: In order for pyruvate, the product of glycolysis, to enter the next pathway, it must undergo several changes.
The conversion is a three-step process (Figure 7.10).
Step 1. A carboxyl group is removed from pyruvate, releasing a molecule of carbon dioxide into the surrounding medium.
This reaction creates a two-carbon hydroxyethyl group bound to the enzyme (pyruvate dehydrogenase).
We should note that this is the first of the six carbons from the original glucose molecule to be removed.

This step proceeds twice because there are two pyruvate molecules produced at the end of glycolysis for every molecule of glucose metabolized anaerobically; thus, two of the six carbons will have been removed at the end of both steps.
Step 2. The hydroxyethyl group is oxidized to an acetyl group, and the electrons are picked up by NAD+, forming NADH.
Step 3. The enzyme-bound acetyl group is transferred to CoA, producing a molecule of acetyl CoA.

grade10.text: Pyruvate, made during glycolysis, has to be changed before it can enter the next pathway.
This change happens in three steps.
First, a carboxyl group is removed from pyruvate and released as carbon dioxide.
This leaves a two-carbon group attached to the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase.
It is the first of the glucose molecule's six carbons to be removed.
The step runs twice per glucose because glycolysis makes two pyruvates, so two carbons are removed.
Second, the two-carbon group is oxidized to an acetyl group, and NAD+ picks up electrons to become NADH.
Third, the acetyl group is passed to CoA, making acetyl CoA.

grade6.text: Pyruvate must change before it can go on.
Step one: a carbon is taken off pyruvate.
It leaves the body as carbon dioxide gas.
A two-carbon piece stays stuck to an enzyme.
This is the first of glucose's six carbons to leave.
Step two: the piece changes form and gives away electrons.
NAD+ catches the electrons and becomes NADH.
Step three: the piece moves to CoA to make acetyl CoA.

glossary.plain: The product of glycolysis, made from glucose.
The first way cells break glucose down.
A small group of atoms with one carbon and two oxygens.
A two-carbon piece left after the first step.
A helper molecule that picks up electrons.
NAD+ after it has picked up electrons.
The final product that enters the next pathway.

quiz.q: Why does step 1 happen twice per glucose?
